children.text: The NGV unit model is a comprehensive, data-driven molecular model of the neuroglia-vascular system built to explore the complex relationships between the aging brain, energy metabolism, blood flow, and neuronal activity. The model includes all key enzymes, transporters, metabolites, and circulatory factors vital for neuronal electrical activity. It is simulated using the Julia scientific computing language.

notebook.description: This data-driven molecular model of the neuro-glia-vascular system allows exploration of the complex relationships between the aging brain, energy metabolism, blood flow, and neuronal activity. Comprising 16,800 interaction pathways, the model includes all key enzymes, transporters, metabolites, and circulatory factors vital for neuronal electrical activity. The simulation allows one to track the time evolution of metabolites in response to a pulse stimulus.
notebook.name: Dynamical model of metabolism, electrophysiology and blood flow in the NGV unit

children.text: This data-driven molecular model of the neuro-glia-vascular system allows exploration of the complex relationships between the aging brain, energy metabolism, blood flow, and neuronal activity. Comprising 16,800 interaction pathways, the model includes all key enzymes,transporters, metabolites, and circulatory factors vital for neuronal electrical activity. The simulation allows one to track the time evolution of metabolites in response to a pulse stimulus.
Download the analysis_notebook.ipynb notebook to your local machine.
Ensure that Julia version 1.6.6 is installed. This can either be done from the command line or by uncommenting the first code cell and running it from the notebook (by Ctrl+Enter or ⌘+Enter).
Add the packages listed in analysis_info.json requirements. The packages can also be installed by uncommenting the codeblock containing Pkg.add and running the cell from the notebook.
Run the notebook. Interactive checkbox sections allow one to select which species are plotted.

You can directly modify parameters and initial values of variables in the downloaded json files. The functions can also be adapted to your needs and run the simulations for your special version of the model.

The related publication is: Polina Shichkova1, Jay Coggan, Lida Kanari, Elvis Boci, Cyrille Favreau, Stefano M. Antonel, Daniel Keller, and Henry Markram. "Breakdown and repair of the aging brain metabolic system" Frontiers in Science, February 2025.

children.text: This project is a starting point and proof of concept for the study of proximal and distal inhibition. We simulate the two cases on the single cell level at various inhibition strengths and compare to what degree the two types of inhibition are capable of preventing the initiation of somatic action potentials.
This project depicts a starting point for the development of a more extensive study. Alternatively, it can be used to illustrate some concepts in an educational context.

It has long been known that different types of cortical inhibitory neurons target different dendritic locationsof postsynaptic neurons. While Basket Cells perform inhibition close to the soma (proximal inhibition), other types - such as somatostatin-positive neurons – target compartments further away (distal inhibition). Various theories exist about their different computational roles.

Here, we simply investigate the following: Considering two inhibitory synaptic input streams that are equivalent in all respects except their dendritic targeting zone, how do they differ in their effect on somatic spiking.
We conduct this study in the following steps.
First, we need to pick a simulatable neuron to study. In the prepared examples, we used a L5 PC model from rat somatosensory areas. All steps can be repeated for other models.

We need to create excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs streams that we can activate. We plan to place 1000 excitatory synapses, 250 proximal inhibitory synapses and 250 distal inhibitory synapses. To that end, we need to know how those numbers translate into a density in terms of synapses per um of dendritic length. This is performed by analyzing the picked morphology. It is performed and further explained in the notebook "Count proximal vs. distal dendritic length".

We then create a “Synaptome model” of the picked simulatable neuron. That is a model comprising the neuron and any number of groups of synaptic inputs. Six groups are created: Excitation, proximal inhibition and distal inhibition, each on basal and apical dendrites. For the purpose of this example, we used 100 um from the soma as a hard cutoff between proximal and distal. A user can easily change this value or use a softer cutoff.
A baseline simulation is run that activates one of the excitatory inputs with various frequencies.
Two additional simulations are run, where the excitatory input is activated with a fixed frequency, and one of the inhibitory inputs is activated with various frequencies.

An analysis of the simulation results is performed to count the number of spikes evoked in each of the simulations. We then plot the number of spikes against the excitatory and inhibitory input frequencies.

In this notebook, we compare the effect of proximal vs. distal inhibition on spike counts of a neuron receiving excitatory inputs. It takes the results of three single neurons synaptome simulatons as inputs:
One where only the excitatory synaptic inputs of the neuron were activated with various frequencies
One where the excitatory inputs were activated at a given frequency, and concurrently the
inhibitory inputs were activated at various frequencies
One as #2 abovey, but for the
instead of the proximal inhibitory inputs.
It then creates two plots: One of excitatory input frequency vs. output spike count, and one of inhibitory input frequencies vs. output spike counts.
In the first cell, fill in the following:
The path to the results of the simulation with excitatory inputs only as "exc-only".
The path to the results of the simulation combining excitatory inputs with proximal inhibition as "inh-prox".
The path to the results of the simulation combining excitatory inputs with distal inhibition as "inh-dist".
The excitatory input frequency used for the simulations combining excitatory inputs with inhibitory inputs as "freq_e_used"

children.text: We distinguish proximal vs. distal innervation on a dendrite by the path distance of a synapse to the post-synaptic soma. This uses an arbitray cutoff, such as 100 um. In order to study the effects of proximal vs distal innervation, it is useful to know how much dendritic length lies between such cutoffs. This allows for more systematic control of variables (such as afferent synapse densities) later on. This notebook provides that functionality.
Simply run the cells of the notebook.
Single Neurons are the building blocks of the nervous system and the brain. Accurate construction of single neuron models is essential to build realistic brain circuits and whole brain models.
This project shows single neuron models (artifacts) and notebooks for different brain regions. Currently, we have biophysically detailed single neurons models for the following brain regions:

We have also created some detailed morphology and simplified neuron canonical models used for whole brain simulations. Canonical models are general models that are available to be used for any brain region. They are annotated with the root brain region known as
The platform currently has a total of
which you can simulate with current injections and synaptic inputs.
We can also build new single neuron models by combining a morphology and an existing e-model. The resulting model is called a

The first video shows how you can Build and Simulate a me-model on the platform. The video demonstrates how to build a somatosensory cortex layer 5 (L5) pyramidal neuron of continuous-accommodating (cADpyr) electrical firing type (e-type). We use a L5 TPC:A (layer 5 thick tufted late bifurcating pyramidal cell) morphology type (m-type) and canonical cADpyr model. You can add recording electrodes at different locations to observe the voltage recordings e.g. on various locations on the apical dendrites. We simulate the me-model with a series of step current injections.
We can also apply excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs on a me-model. A me-model with all its synaptic inputs is called a

The second video shows how we Build a Synaptome with the pyramidal neuron me-model created in the first video and then Simulate the me-model with step current injection series. We add excitatory synapses on the apical dendrites with a formula of 0.003*x synapses/µm where x is the distance from soma in µm. You can also exclude placing synapses up to some distance from soma. Similarly, we also add inhibitory synapses to basal dendrites and save the synaptome. Now, we can Simulate the Synaptome, by activating both synaptic inputs and specifying their parameters and adding step current injections.
The third video shows the e-models registered on the platform. The e-models were built using our e-model building python pipeline,

. E-model page shows the configuration used for various steps of the model building pipeline: e-feature extraction, e-model optimisation and validation and with analysis figures including optimisation evolution, currrent scape and optimisation features, traces among others among others. These e-models are not simulatable.

The fourth video shows how to simulate pre-built me-models and synaptomes on the platform. We select me-model list in Explore section of the platform. Then, we inject multiple step current injections in the soma and record soma and dendritic action potentials.
You can also select and simulate pre-built Synaptome models from "Explore". Select an existing synaptome model and simulate it.

notebook.description: Compare parameters of an single cell electrical model (e-model) across cell sections.
notebook.name: Model parameter comparison plot

children.text: Parameter comparison plots among section of an e-model
Author: Darshan Mandge, Open Brain Institute
Notebook to compare final parameter values for different sections such as apical, basal dendrites and soma of a single cell electrical model (e-model).
The goal of this notebook is to compare and understand the relation between different paramteres in an e-model
An e-model is usually constructed from intracellular patch clamp data using multi-objective optimisation
We use the Open Brain Institute (OBI) Platform and our single cell modelling pipeline:
The pipeline performs the following steps:
extraction of electrical features (e-features) from the electrophysiology data
optimisation of the e-features to minimise the z-score of each feature and reduce the overall e-model score (sum of e-feature z-scores)
The pipeline store the final e-model details in a json file (EM__*.json) containing details such as
: the e-model score (sum of e-feature z-scores)
: the hall of fame (best) parameters values which are were selected for different sections of the detailed morphology.
: selected seed value from the multiple optimisation runs
The data downloading is done in the notebook. Simply follow the instructions there.

children.text: This notebook demonstrates how to compute and plot the IV (current-voltage) and FI (frequency-current) curves for single cell model using BlueCelluLab. These analyses provide insights into the neuron’s electrical properties, such as its input resistance, firing threshold, and response to varying levels of stimulation. The notebook also explains how to set different injection and recording locations to study various neuron behaviors, like dendritic integration, backpropagation, and somatic excitability, through IV and FI curve analyses.
In order to run this notebook, you will have to install the dependencies listed in analysis_info.json in requirements.

notebook.description: Explains how to use traces from voltage clamp in eFEL to extract efeatures for ion channel construction
notebook.name: Voltage clamp efeature extraction

children.text: Author: Darshan Mandge, Open Brain Institute
This notebook demonstrates how to load electrophysiology data using h5py for eFEL e-features extraction. We will use a NWB data voltage clamp experiments on cells expressing an ion channel gene.
The NWB data file contains experimental data from patch clamp experiments as described in

The experiments were performed on cells from cell lines such as Chinese hamster ovary (CHO). The CHO cells do not have their own native channel expressed. Individual ion channel genes cloned from rat/mouse are expressed in these cells and automated patch clamp recordings are performed on these cells.
is from Cell line: CHO FT rKv1.1. The gene expressed is for Kv1.1 ion channel cloned from rat cells. The recordings were made at 25 degree celsius.
The patched cells were held at different voltage clamp levels and the intracellular currents were recorded for activation, inactivation and deactivation properties of the ion channels.
The goal of this notebook is to extract features for these properties which are then useful to construct ion channels.

If the number that passed plus the number that failed is lower than the number of morphologies loaded, it indicates that a test failed to run to completion.
